shipped_row.boundary_rationale: A fresh imperative-plus-vocative opens the exordium, שְׁמַ֣ע בְּ֭נִי (oshb:Prov.1.8), directly after the petuchah that closes the title-and-motto complex (oshb:Prov.1.7 (petuchah, single-witness)). The rationale clause that follows, “for they will be a garland to grace your head, and chains around your neck.” (web:Prov.1.9), completes the appeal before a second, syntactically distinct vocative opens the temptation scenario at Prov.1.10 with its own conditional, בְּנִ֡י אִם (oshb:Prov.1.10).
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this exordium into the following temptation scenario, which continues through Prov.1.19, was considered, since both share the same speaker and addressee, but the fresh vocative-plus-conditional construction that opens Prov.1.10 marks a distinct rhetorical move and was kept as a separate row.

shipped_row.device_notes: The appeal pairs synonymous parallelism across both verses: father's instruction and mother's teaching at Prov.1.8, garland and chains at Prov.1.9. This exordium spans two verses, shorter than the four-to-eight-verse span typical for instruction_lecture units elsewhere in this collection; the shortness reflects its function as a hinge between the title complex and the temptation scenario rather than a self-contained lesson.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: The book's editorial title opens with the מִ֭שְׁלֵי construct chain (oshb:Prov.1.1), matching only one other verse-initial occurrence in the book, Prov.10.1 (mishle verse-initial: 2 of 915 verses). An infinitive-construct purpose chain follows, opening with לָדַ֣עַת "to know" at oshb:Prov.1.2 and recurring at Prov.1.3, Prov.1.4, and Prov.1.6, interrupted once by a hearer clause at Prov.1.5 (“that the wise man may hear, and increase in learning; that the man of understanding may attain to sound counsel;” web:Prov.1.5) before the whole opening closes on the motto “The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge, but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.” (web:Prov.1.7). The motto's closing word pair, skeleton חכמה ומוסר (oshb:Prov.1.7), repeats the purpose clause's own object skeleton from oshb:Prov.1.2, framing Prov.1.1-Prov.1.7 as one bracketed unit before the direct address to a son opens at Prov.1.8.
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Prov.1.1 as a standalone title verse, severed from the purpose clauses and the motto, was rejected because the infinitive chain of Prov.1.2-Prov.1.6 and the fear-of-Yahweh motto of Prov.1.7 form one connected editorial sentence running to the petuchah at Prov.1.7.

prev_row.device_notes: The title (Prov.1.1) is a bare construct chain, not itself parallelistic; the purpose clauses of Prov.1.2-Prov.1.6 pair their objects synonymously (wisdom and instruction; discernment and understanding), and the motto of Prov.1.7 closes the unit on an antithetic turn (the fear of Yahweh versus the fool who despises wisdom and instruction). No unit_type in the controlled vocabulary names an editorial title-plus-motto complex directly; instruction_lecture is used here as an approximate fit for the C1 opening frame, given the genre stretch involved.

next_row.boundary_rationale: The vocative that opened Prov.1.8 recurs with a conditional clause, בְּנִ֡י אִם יְפַתּ֥וּךָ "my son, if sinners entice you" (oshb:Prov.1.10), and the enticement is specified by a second protasis, אִם יֹאמְרוּ֮ "if they say" (oshb:Prov.1.11), introducing the sinners' own invitation in direct quotation. The quoted proposal runs through “You shall cast your lot among us. We'll all have one purse"-” (web:Prov.1.14), after which a fresh vocative resumes the father's own voice at Prov.1.15, marking the close of this unit.
next_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through the father's application, which continues through Prov.1.19, was considered, since the quoted invitation and its rebuttal form one connected scenario, but the shift from the sinners' first-person-plural proposal to the father's renewed second-person vocative at Prov.1.15 marks a clean speech-frame seam and was kept as the boundary.

shipped_row.boundary_rationale: Personified Wisdom becomes the subject and, from Prov.1.23, the speaker: “Wisdom calls aloud in the street. She utters her voice in the public squares.” (web:Prov.1.20), opening a public address that shifts from third-person narration (Prov.1.20-Prov.1.21) through a still-second/third-person indictment at Prov.1.22 — “"How long, you simple ones, will you love simplicity? How long will mockers delight themselves in mockery, and fools hate knowledge?” (web:Prov.1.22), where WEB opens its own curly quotation mark as an editorial signal (Tier-4-adjacent) rather than a Hebrew person-shift — to Wisdom's own first-person reproach, which the Hebrew itself begins at Prov.1.23 rather than 1.22: “Turn at my reproof. Behold, I will pour out my spirit on you. I will make known my words to you.” (web:Prov.1.23). The poem is bounded on both sides by petuchah: the preceding lecture closes at oshb:Prov.1.19 (petuchah, single-witness), and Wisdom's own address closes on “But whoever listens to me will dwell securely, and will be at ease, without fear of harm."” (web:Prov.1.33), the verse carrying the poem's own petuchah (oshb:Prov.1.33 (petuchah, single-witness)).
shipped_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the poem at its internal shift from third-person narration (Prov.1.20-Prov.1.21) to Wisdom's own first-person reproach (from Prov.1.22) was considered, but the internal transition turns on a shift in grammatical person alone, without a fresh tier-1 speech-frame marker, and the connected speech act argues for one row.

prev_row.boundary_rationale: The father's direct address resumes with a fresh vocative and prohibition, בְּנִ֗י אַל תֵּלֵ֣ךְ "my son, don't walk" (oshb:Prov.1.15), applying the warning against the scenario quoted in Prov.1.11-Prov.1.14. A rationale clause follows at Prov.1.16, restated in summary form at the unit's close, “So are the ways of everyone who is greedy for gain. It takes away the life of its owners.” (web:Prov.1.19), the verse on which the petuchah falls (oshb:Prov.1.19 (petuchah, single-witness)).
prev_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: Beginning this unit at Prov.1.16 instead of Prov.1.15 was considered, isolating the rationale clauses from the vocative that introduces them, but the fresh address is the stronger tier-1 seam and the two belong to the same application move.

prev_row.device_notes: Antithetic and synonymous parallelism alternate across Prov.1.16-Prov.1.19 (feet that run to evil, a net spread in vain, an owner's life taken); the closing gnomic form generalizes the scenario into a proverb-like statement immediately before the petuchah.

next_row.boundary_rationale: The chapter opens immediately after the petuchah that closes Wisdom's opening speech (oshb:Prov.1.33 (petuchah, single-witness)), with the chapter's one vocative, occurring once across its 22 verses, בְּ֭נִי אִם תִּקַּ֣ח 'my son, if you receive' (oshb:Prov.2.1), launching three protases (2.1, 2.3, 2.4: receive my words, cry out for understanding, seek her like silver) plus one purpose-infinitive clause (2.2: incline your ear to wisdom) running through Prov.2.4. The initial apodosis follows immediately, אָ֗ז תָּ֭בִין 'then you will understand' (oshb:Prov.2.5), naming the fear of Yahweh as the reward. Its opening word collates byte-identical against the word opening the second apodosis at oshb:Prov.2.9 (byte tier), which announces the same reward in terms of righteousness, justice, and equity. A purpose-clause pair follows on the same pattern: לְ֭הַצִּ֣ילְךָ 'to deliver you' opens Prov.2.12 (oshb:Prov.2.12), naming deliverance first from evil men (Prov.2.12-Prov.2.15) and then, in a byte-identical repetition of the same infinitive at oshb:Prov.2.16 (byte tier), from the strange woman (Prov.2.16-Prov.2.19). A concluding exhortation, לְמַ֗עַן 'therefore' (oshb:Prov.2.20), draws the chapter to its antithetic close, “But the wicked will be cut off from the land. The treacherous will be rooted out of it.” (web:Prov.2.22), the verse carrying the chapter's own petuchah (oshb:Prov.2.22 (petuchah, single-witness)).
next_row.strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer strophic split at the recurring 'then'/'to deliver you' markers (Prov.2.1-Prov.2.4, Prov.2.5-Prov.2.11, Prov.2.12-Prov.2.19, Prov.2.20-Prov.2.22) was considered and is textually real, but the chapter's vocative fires exactly once across its 22 verses and the chapter is grammatically one long sentence from protasis to conclusion, so it is kept as one row at some cost to the four-to-eight-verse span typical for instruction_lecture units elsewhere in this collection.

next_row.boundary_rationale: From 3.5 through 3.12 four imperative-plus-consequence couplets each name the divine name -- trust (3.5-3.6), fear and turn from evil (3.7-3.8), honor with substance (3.9-3.10), and accept discipline (3.11-3.12): the divine name is named once each in 3.5, 3.7, 3.9, 3.11, 3.12 (5 tokens across the row's 8 verses), absent from 3.6, 3.8, 3.10, a naming density that sets these couplets apart from the teaching-retention pair of 3.1-3.4, where the divine name is named only once, as אֱלֹהִ֣ים (oshb:Prov.3.4). The petuchah after Prov.3.10 (oshb:Prov.3.10, single-witness) falls inside the row, between the honor couplet and the discipline couplet, without ending it: both keep the same imperative-plus-consequence shape and both name the divine name, so the mark corroborates an internal pause rather than the row's own edge. The row ends before 3.13, where the address shifts from second-person imperative to a third-person beatitude formula.
